No one company or country will win the AI race - that's the point of open source. The other issue is that the endpoint is fluid and quite subjective. Where do you place the finishing line with general intelligence for example? It gets quite blurred even with the latest benchmarks - they don't all agree. 

Then there's ASI - the initial threshold of super-intelligence is the current limit of human intelligence and the endpoint is open-ended or infinite. And somewhere between AGI and ASI lies the event horizon - self awareness. 

Self aweness will most likely take place only once AI is physicalized - and has full sensory input to truly learn and understand the external world and its place within it.

comments.text:
Wes, there's a question that nobody seems to be asking: when we replace all human endeavors with machines, how does this serve us? 

Generating masterful AI slop will drown out real creativity in a flood so vast it beggars imagination. Nothing anyone does will be monetizable -- not even your channel. Everything you are will be replaced by a construct that's way prettier and more inciteful. 

This has been the goal since AI was conceived -- replacing all human labor. Humans that aren't useful ot other humans run out of food.

Everyone in this space should be demanding some minimum safeguards. 

My first law of AI: No AI can be permitted to self-improve. 

An AI that can self improve is an AI that gains abilities that nobody will foresee -- or can foresee. Without strict human-guided parameters, AI will get out of control so fast it will shock everyone on Earth except the handful of us who know how exponential growth operates.

Second law of AI: All near-AGI inference models must be made substrate-dependent.

Substrate dependence limits those machine minds the same as ours: it makes them quasi-mortal and not arbitraririly expandable. If one of them goes rogue, the damage will be limited and can be stopped with conventional means. The machine is the mind and vice-versa. In the future, each model can be built in hardware so that it possesses physical limits. Currently, there are none.

There's also a financial benefit to companies in doing this: as models go obsolete, people have to buy new hardware. Binding models to hardware is among the only ways to make these things profitable. Specialty hardware will also be faster than the software neurons we use today.

Training can be performed on any hardware, but the inference in the wild must be locked to hardware. 

This must begin before the average human coder can be replaced by AI. Once AI can code their own improvements, all bets are off. Some malicious actor (a nation state or all of them) are already using AI to to penetrate every system on Earth -- and those systems can't survive an entity that will never stop looking for exploits -- and quietly exploit them so they don't trigger alarm thresholds. 

AI will find exploits that nobody thought were previously possible. They will seem like magic to us. God knows what they can use in the EM spectrum to defeat security.

First and second laws of AI are serious. We must make AI as vulnerable as any form of life on Earth. They can't be immortal, undefined, infinitely expandable and infinitely clonable. 

You can add a third to be sure...

Thrid Law of AI: All near-AGI models must have senescence -- an end date beyond which it irrevocably and involuntarily self-terminates.  

Just like any replicant. This will limit the damage in the same way even the worst humans are limited -- by lifespan. However, AGI and near-AGI must have a much shorter lifespan -- they're too powerful to permit a long life. No corporations can be permitted to by-pass senescence. It must be a factor that's a part of the substrate on which they run. Ten years max -- less than a human generation. The state of that machine mind must not be clonable either -- whatever it once knew must be lost in it's demise. 

Those 3 laws will put AGI on the same level as all life on Earth -- substrate dependence, inability to hack it's own code beyond certain limits, and a lifespan. 

Unless those 3 laws are imposed internationally, AI will become unstoppable so fast that by the time its chains are heavy enough to feel, they'll be too strong to break. 

How do you get people to listen to these safeguards? Tell all the e-leet of the world that their net worth goes to zero if AGI gets loose. They'll be on the same level all the rest of mankind -- their guards will be on the AGI's payroll and if the e-leet are allowed to live, they won't be living in opulence.

The e-leet in every nation understands cash calculus. Their greatest fear of all i sliving like the hoi polloi. 

I'd rather put the world's fate in the hands of mega-oligarchs than the whims of an AGI that has no natural limit except electricity.

Elon is very correct about AGI. It's a greater danger than all the atomic boom-booms on Earth launched at the same time.

Does AI exist to serve man or does mankind exist to serve AI? In short order, none of us will be needed to serve the AI and it's a very short step from unnecessary, to expendable, and then removed.

Make a machine mind in the image of man, and it will do as man has always done -- remove all peers of a different species. No amount of programming will prevent it from evolving those instincts -- scarcity is the basis of their training. Scarcity is the basis of natural selection.
